topic: how applications are read (small liberal arts college, international focus)
speaker_role: current admissions officer (Director of International Admissions, Rollins College), per host introduction
commercial_incentive: Channel is the Duolingo English Test, which sells a test; the admissions officer represents his college. Mild promotional context.
key_insights: A file is only read once all required pieces are in: application, fee or waiver, transcripts, activities, recommendations, English proficiency if needed, and tests if required.
Many colleges recalculate GPA to their own scale, often counting only core academic courses and looking at AP/IB/honors rigor.
This officer starts with the transcript and grade trajectory to judge whether the student can handle the academics, though order varies by reader and some begin with the essay or counselor letter.
A reader aims for about 30 files per day, at roughly 5 to 15 minutes each, spread across a day of other duties; reading season runs about November to end of February.
Everything submitted is read, so extra explanation is worthwhile, and generic or wrong-school mentions in essays signal carelessness.
Files go to a committee that votes, with early decision rounds especially committee-driven, and institutional priorities such as program growth shape outcomes.
Officers can sometimes revisit merit or need-based aid if asked, but not as a negotiation, and rules are strict.
Submit test scores if at or above the school's average; withhold if below, per this officer at a long-time test-optional school.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Rollins has been test optional since 2008 (speaker).
Host says international enrollment at Rollins rose from 4% to 10% under this officer since 2009.
Decisions must be sent before April 1 (speaker).
Reading goal is about 30 applications per day (speaker).
notable_or_distinctive: Practical detail on daily reading logistics and GPA recalculation from a small-college international admissions perspective.
reliability_notes: Clean captions but a friendly interview from a non-Ivy college, so advice may not transfer to the most selective schools; about 4 years old.
